meta.note: Every quantity is a number with a unit, a year and a source_id. Rank is derived at runtime, never stored.

discovered.era: Priestley and Scheele, independently

facts.text: Almost half the mass of the Earth's crust is oxygen — it is locked into silicate rock, not floating in the air.
By mass the crust is closer to a foam of oxygen atoms held apart by silicon than to anything metallic.

annualProduction.note: silicon materials: ferrosilicon plus silicon metal

discovered.era: Isolated by Berzelius

facts.text: Semiconductor-grade silicon is refined to 99.9999999% purity — nine nines, among the purest bulk materials ever made.
Second only to oxygen in the crust, and the two are usually found bonded to each other as silica.

anthropogenicStock.note: in-use stock, part of the 39 Gt metals category

annualProduction.note: primary smelter production

discovered.era: Ørsted; commercially viable after Hall–Héroult, 1886

facts.text: Recycling aluminium takes about 5% of the energy needed to smelt it from ore, and the metal loses nothing in the process.
Before electrolysis made it cheap, aluminium outpriced gold; Napoleon III reserved aluminium cutlery for his most honoured guests.

annualProduction.note: blast-furnace pig iron, the feedstock for most steel

discovered.era: Iron Age; meteoric iron worked far earlier

facts.text: Iron is the most abundant element in the Earth as a whole — most of it sank into the core while the planet was still molten.
Every iron atom heavier than nickel in your blood was forged in a dying star; the crust merely inherited it.

discovered.era: Isolated by Humphry Davy

facts.text: Calcium reaches the crust mostly as limestone — the compressed remains of shells and skeletons.
Cement is essentially a way of un-making limestone with heat and then letting it set again.

discovered.era: Isolated by Humphry Davy

facts.text: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife and light enough to float on water — briefly, and violently.
Nearly all the sodium humans handle arrives as salt, either mined or evaporated from the sea.

discovered.era: Isolated by Humphry Davy

facts.text: Magnesium is the lightest structural metal in common use — about two-thirds the density of aluminium.
Seawater holds roughly 1.3 kg of magnesium per tonne, which is where a good share of production comes from.

discovered.era: Isolated by Humphry Davy — the first metal won by electrolysis

facts.text: Potassium is mildly radioactive: about one atom in ten thousand is potassium-40, which is why bananas register on a sensitive detector.
Most mined potassium becomes fertiliser — the K in NPK.

annualProduction.note: titanium sponge metal; titanium mineral concentrates run ~9 Mt/yr

discovered.era: Identified by Gregor; pure metal isolated 1910

facts.text: Titanium is the ninth most abundant element in the crust, yet it stayed a laboratory curiosity for a century because separating it from oxygen is brutally hard.
The SR-71 Blackbird was 85% titanium, and much of the ore was bought through intermediaries from the Soviet Union.

discovered.era: Prehistoric — charcoal, soot and diamond all known to antiquity

facts.text: Carbon is a rounding error in the crust at 200 ppm, and simultaneously the backbone of every living thing.
Graphite and diamond are the same element; the difference is entirely how the atoms are stacked.
All living things together hold about 550 gigatonnes of carbon — and human-made mass now outweighs the lot.

annualProduction.note: almost all of it made from fossil gas and used for ammonia and refining

discovered.era: Henry Cavendish

facts.text: Hydrogen is by far the most abundant element in the universe and a bit player in the crust, where it hides inside water and clay.
Counting atoms rather than mass, hydrogen is roughly 15% of the crust — it is just extremely light.

discovered.era: Hennig Brand, by boiling down urine

facts.text: Phosphorus has no substitute in agriculture: there is no other element that does its job in DNA and ATP.
It was the first element discovered since antiquity, and it was found by a man searching urine for gold.

anthropogenicStock.note: in-use stock worldwide, roughly 4–5 t per person in industrialised countries

tensileStrength.note: mild steel; alloy steels reach 2 GPa

discovered.era: Bessemer converter; crucible and wootz steels far older

facts.text: Steel is the most recycled material on Earth by mass — around 90% of it comes back at end of life.
Making it accounts for roughly 7–9% of global CO2 emissions, almost all of it from using coal to strip oxygen off iron.

anthropogenicStock.note: in-use stock, part of the metals category

annualProduction.note: mine production, copper content

discovered.era: The first metal humans worked, found native in usable lumps

facts.text: Copper kills bacteria on contact, which is why hospital door handles are quietly going back to brass.
Electrifying everything runs on copper: a wind turbine holds several tonnes of it, an EV about four times what a petrol car needs.

annualProduction.note: mine production, zinc content

discovered.era: Isolated by Marggraf; brass made for millennia before

facts.text: Over half of all zinc goes into galvanising — a sacrificial skin that corrodes so the steel underneath does not.
Zinc is the third metal your body needs most, after iron and, arguably, calcium.

annualProduction.note: mine production, lead content

discovered.era: Smelted in Anatolia; the Romans plumbed cities with it

facts.text: Around 85% of lead now goes into batteries, and lead-acid batteries are recycled at over 95% — the highest rate of any consumer product.
Ice cores record Roman smelting: atmospheric lead rose across the Empire and fell with it.

annualProduction.note: mine production, nickel content

discovered.era: Cronstedt, from an ore miners called 'Old Nick's copper'

facts.text: Nickel is what makes stainless steel stainless — most of it never appears as nickel at all.
The Earth's core is roughly a twentieth nickel, alloyed with iron.

annualProduction.note: mine production, tin content

discovered.era: Bronze Age — tin plus copper started it

facts.text: Tin is scarce and unevenly spread, so Bronze Age trade routes ran thousands of kilometres to fetch it.
Almost half of today's tin is solder — the metal that physically holds electronics together.

anthropogenicStock.note: all gold ever mined, still above ground

discovered.era: Worked from native nuggets before any smelting existed

facts.text: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 metres on a side — a single suburban house, filled solid.
One gram can be beaten into a sheet a square metre across, thin enough to see daylight through.
Almost none of it is thrown away; the gold in a Roman coin is probably still in circulation as something else.

discovered.era: Cupellation from lead ores in Anatolia

facts.text: Silver conducts heat and electricity better than any other element — copper only wins on price.
Solar panels are now one of the largest single consumers of silver, as paste printed onto every cell.

annualProduction.note: lithium content, excluding US production withheld by USGS

discovered.era: Arfwedson, in a Swedish mineral

facts.text: Lithium is the least dense solid element — it floats on oil, let alone water.
Production has roughly tripled since 2018, driven almost entirely by batteries.

annualProduction.note: usable ore, gross weight

discovered.era: Banded iron formations laid down 2.5 billion years ago

facts.text: Most iron ore was deposited when the first photosynthesising microbes rusted the oceans — an atmospheric catastrophe we now mine.
It is the second-largest bulk cargo on Earth by tonnage moved, after coal.

discovered.era: Named for Les Baux-de-Provence, where it was first described

facts.text: Bauxite is tropical soil that has been rained on for millions of years until only aluminium and iron oxides remain.
It takes roughly four tonnes of bauxite to make one tonne of aluminium, and the leftover red mud is one of the largest industrial waste streams in the world.

annualProduction.note: estimate: limestone quarried for cement, lime and aggregate; not reported as a single global statistic

discovered.era: Quarried since the Pyramids; formed from marine shells over hundreds of millions of years

facts.text: Limestone is mostly the compressed bodies of sea creatures — the White Cliffs of Dover are a graveyard of plankton.
Burning it to make cement releases CO2 that was captured by those organisms; that chemistry alone is about half of cement's emissions.

discovered.era: Mined and traded since the Neolithic

facts.text: Only a small fraction of mined salt is eaten; most goes into chlorine and caustic soda, or onto winter roads.
Salt was money: 'salary' comes from the Roman allowance for buying it.

discovered.era: Used as plaster at Çatalhöyük, ~7000 BCE

facts.text: Gypsum board resists fire because the water chemically bound inside it must boil off before the panel can get hotter than about 100 °C.
Alabaster, plaster of Paris and the walls of most modern houses are all the same mineral in different states of hydration.

annualProduction.note: mostly recovered as a by-product of refining oil and gas

discovered.era: Known to antiquity; named as an element by Lavoisier, 1777

facts.text: Almost no sulfur is mined any more — it is stripped out of fossil fuels to stop acid rain, then sold.
Sulfuric acid made from it is the single largest-volume industrial chemical on the planet, and most of it makes fertiliser.

discovered.era: First patented as superphosphate fertiliser by Lawes

facts.text: About 70% of the world's phosphate reserves sit in a single country, Morocco, including Western Sahara.
Roughly half the people alive are fed by crops grown with mined phosphate; there is no synthetic substitute.

anthropogenicStock.note: aggregates in place, the second-largest human-made stock after concrete

annualProduction.note: 50 Gt/yr of sand, gravel and crushed stone; the most-extracted solid material on Earth

discovered.era: The ground itself

facts.text: Humans move more sand and gravel than every river on Earth combined.
Desert sand is useless for concrete — wind-rounded grains will not lock together — which is why Dubai imports sand.
It is the second-most consumed resource after water, and almost entirely unregulated.

discovered.era: Joseph Aspdin patents Portland cement; Roman pozzolana far older

facts.text: Cement production is about 8% of global CO2 emissions — more than aviation and shipping together.
China poured more cement in three years than the United States did in the entire twentieth century.

anthropogenicStock.note: the single largest human-made mass on Earth

annualProduction.note: estimated from cement output at roughly 1:7 by mass. Cement is measured; concrete is not.

tensileStrength.note: about a tenth of its compressive strength — hence rebar

discovered.era: Roman opus caementicium; Portland-cement concrete from 1824

facts.text: There is more concrete on Earth than there are trees, animals and people put together — by mass it outweighs all living things.
Roman harbour concrete gets stronger as seawater reacts with volcanic ash inside it; modern concrete does the opposite.
Nobody measures concrete directly. Every figure you have ever read is cement production multiplied by an assumption.

annualProduction.note: derived from the growth rate of the brick stock; no single global statistic exists

discovered.era: Sun-dried mud brick in the Levant; fired brick by ~3000 BCE

facts.text: Fired brick is one of the oldest manufactured materials still in daily use, essentially unchanged for five thousand years.
The standard brick size survives because it is what one hand can pick up.

annualProduction.note: container plus flat glass; industry estimate, not an official statistic

meltingPoint.note: working temperature; glass has no true melting point

discovered.era: Mesopotamia; float glass invented 1959

facts.text: Glass is not a slow-flowing liquid. Old cathedral panes are uneven because of how they were spun, not because they sagged.
It can be recycled endlessly with no loss of quality, and a recycled bottle can be back on a shelf within a month.

annualProduction.note: tiles, sanitaryware, tableware and refractories; industry estimate

thermalConductivity.note: wide range: 2 W/(m·K) for porcelain, 150+ for aluminium nitride

discovered.era: Fired clay figurines from Dolní Věstonice

facts.text: The oldest fired ceramic objects are not pots but figurines, made 26,000 years ago — art preceded tableware by fifteen millennia.
Boron carbide plate stops rifle rounds at a third the weight of the steel that would be needed.

annualProduction.note: a record year

discovered.era: Burned in Bronze Age China and Roman Britain; industrialised from 1700s

facts.text: Most coal formed in a single 60-million-year window when trees had evolved lignin but fungi had not yet learned to digest it.
Coal use hit an all-time record in 2023 — the decline everyone forecast has not started yet.

annualProduction.note: about 96 million barrels per day

discovered.era: Drake well, Pennsylvania; seep oil used for millennia

facts.text: Only about 4% of a barrel becomes plastic — but that 4% is where almost every synthetic material in your house comes from.
The world burns roughly 1,500 barrels every second.

annualProduction.note: converted from ~4.1 trillion m³ at 0.717 kg/m³

discovered.era: First commercial well, Fredonia, New York

facts.text: Nearly all industrial hydrogen — and therefore nearly all synthetic fertiliser — is made by tearing apart natural gas.
Methane traps about 80 times more heat than CO2 over its first twenty years in the atmosphere.

annualProduction.note: refinery bitumen output; industry estimate

discovered.era: Used to waterproof Mesopotamian boats and mummies

facts.text: The Pitch Drop Experiment has been running since 1927; bitumen behaves as a solid but flows about one drop per decade.
Asphalt pavement is the most recycled material in the world by weight in several countries — old road is milled straight back into new road.

annualProduction.note: converted from 3.97 billion m³ of roundwood at ~0.65 t/m³ air-dry

density.note: 300–850 depending on species; balsa 170, lignum vitae 1250

discovered.era: Prehistoric — the first structural material

facts.text: Along the grain, wood beats steel on strength for its weight; across the grain it splits in your hands.
About half of all wood cut worldwide is still burned for cooking and heating.
The Hōryū-ji temple in Japan has been standing in wood since 607 CE.

discovered.era: Cai Lun, Han dynasty China

facts.text: The paperless office never arrived; packaging board grew as screens replaced letters, because everything now ships in a box.
A cellulose fibre survives roughly five to seven trips through the recycling loop before it is too short to hold together.

annualProduction.note: wheat, rice, maize and other cereals; grain only, not straw

discovered.era: Domesticated in the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Three grasses — wheat, rice and maize — supply about half of all calories eaten by humans.
Cereal is the largest deliberately harvested flow of biomass on the planet.

annualProduction.note: lint

discovered.era: Domesticated independently in India, Peru and Africa

facts.text: A single cotton fibre is stronger than steel of the same weight when wet — cotton gains strength as it soaks.
Around 10,000 litres of water go into one kilogram of cotton; the Aral Sea was drained largely to grow it.

annualProduction.note: greasy wool

discovered.era: Sheep bred for fleece in Mesopotamia

facts.text: Wool can hold nearly a third of its weight in water and still feel dry, because the moisture binds inside the fibre.
It is naturally flame-resistant — it chars and self-extinguishes rather than melting.

discovered.era: Mesoamerican rubber ballgames by 1600 BCE; Goodyear vulcanises it in 1839

facts.text: No synthetic rubber matches natural latex for heat build-up, so every aircraft and truck tyre still contains tree sap.
Goodyear found vulcanisation by accident, dropping a sulfur-rubber mix on a hot stove.

discovered.era: Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic

facts.text: Around 9% of all plastic ever made has been recycled. Roughly 12% has been burned. The rest still exists.
Humanity has produced over 9 billion tonnes of plastic since 1950, more than half of it since 2004.
Plastic now outweighs all land and marine animals combined.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total

discovered.era: Found by accident at ICI Northwich under extreme pressure

facts.text: Polyethylene is the most-made synthetic material on Earth: bags, bottles, pipe, and the film over every greenhouse.
It was discovered by accident twice, and kept secret during the war because it insulated radar cabling better than anything else.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total

discovered.era: Natta, using Ziegler catalysts — a Nobel followed

facts.text: Polypropylene hinges can flex a million times without breaking, which is why the lid of a shampoo bottle is moulded in one piece.
It floats — one of the few common plastics less dense than water, which is how recycling plants sort it.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total

discovered.era: Observed by Baumann; made workable by Waldo Semon in 1926

facts.text: PVC is over half salt by mass, which makes it the least oil-hungry of the big plastics.
Rigid pipe made from it is expected to last a century underground; the same polymer plasticised becomes a raincoat.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total; excludes polyester fibre

discovered.era: Whinfield and Dickson; the blow-moulded bottle arrives in 1973

facts.text: PET is the only plastic with a genuine bottle-to-bottle recycling loop at scale — and even that mostly ends up as fleece.
Most polyester clothing is the same molecule as a fizzy-drink bottle, spun into thread.

discovered.era: Bayer's methyl rubber; mass-produced during the Second World War

facts.text: The US built a synthetic rubber industry from nothing in three years after Japan took the rubber plantations of South-East Asia.
A car tyre is a composite of a dozen rubbers, steel cord and textile — which is exactly why tyres are so hard to recycle.

annualProduction.note: natural graphite; synthetic graphite adds roughly as much again

thermalConductivity.note: in-plane; about 30 times lower through the sheets

discovered.era: Borrowdale deposit, England — the first pencils

facts.text: Graphite is slippery because its carbon sheets slide over each other; a pencil line is those sheets peeling off one at a time.
The anode of every lithium-ion battery is graphite, so there is more of it in an EV than there is lithium.

annualProduction.note: industry estimate; no official statistic

discovered.era: High-strength process developed at RAE Farnborough

facts.text: A single filament is about 6 micrometres across — roughly a tenth the width of a human hair.
Half the structural mass of a Boeing 787 is carbon composite, which is also why a damaged panel cannot simply be beaten out.
It is essentially unrecyclable: the fibres survive, the epoxy does not, and separating them costs more than new fibre.

annualProduction.note: market estimate, wide error bars; most output is multi-layer flake, not true monolayer

discovered.era: Geim and Novoselov, peeled off graphite with sticky tape

facts.text: A sheet of graphene as thin as cling film could support an elephant standing on a pencil point — if you could make one that big without a single flaw.
It was isolated with ordinary adhesive tape, and that experiment won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Twenty years on, the flaw-free sheet remains the whole problem: production is measured in tonnes, not megatonnes.
